items_missed: No 'how are you today?' or any warm-up. The call went from 'Hi, Larissa! Thank you so much for calling us back' straight to 'let me just pull up your profile first.'

Agenda statement had no timeframe and no confirmation ask. She said 'we actually just wanna ask some questions about this move so we can give you a more personalized estimate but of course I'll send everything in the email as well after our call' — good roadmap, but never 'takes about 10-15 minutes' and never 'sound good?' before launching into the questions.
Storage stops never asked about at either apartment or the destination — the one probe bullet she skipped in an otherwise complete discovery.

No 'pricing is super simple' framing. The transition was 'how we work is that we charge by the hour for all of our services' — functional, but it does not set up the simplicity story before the numbers land.

Save Your Ass prep speech never actually delivered. She stated the principle — 'the shorter than move is gonna be then the lower the cost at the end of the day. So, how prepared we are on...' — and then dropped it mid-sentence to talk about parking. No consolidation examples (kids' toys, garden tools, loose items in drawers, photos off walls), no 'take a carload' tip, and no 'does that make sense?' close on the prep section.

The carload/self-help conversation was customer-initiated, not coached. Clarissa asked 'if I have a dolly and if I asked them to load my [car] could I also help transport stuff' — Joanna answered the policy correctly but never turned it into the pre-move-day carload tip that shortens the billable clock.

Estimate range logic is internally inconsistent. She said 'typically a one bedroom apartment usually takes two and a half to three and a half hours... since we're moving two one bedroom apartments we are already at the range of five to seven hours now that with two guys' and then quoted '$the six to eight hour mark with three men involved.' Adding a third mover extended the range upward instead of compressing it. The walking-distance buffer was the stated reason, but the customer heard a bigger number for more manpower with no arithmetic connecting the two.
Traffic never raised as a time variable on a multi-stop Houston Saturday move with two loading addresses.

No BOLDED-details framing for the confirmation email and no 'reply with any corrections' — she promised 'I'll go ahead and send you an updated quotation so just disregard the initial one' but never told Clarissa to verify the details back.
No 'any other questions before I let you go?' The close was 'I'll talk to you later. Have a good day guys.'
Hours and how to reach us never given. Closest was 'all you have to do is give us a call' with no window and no direct number.

Soft close with no forward step. When Clarissa said 'I think I'll go ahead and talk to my [roommate] but and then we can go' Joanna accepted it with 'Yeah, no, no problem' and did not propose a specific callback time or offer to soft-hold the Saturday she had just called 'the day that books a faster than the rest of the week.'
60¢/lb baseline liability never mentioned alongside No Worries, so the $2,000 coverage had no contrast to make it land.
Wrong name at the farewell — 'Alright, you're welcome. Thanks Teresa.' — on a call where she had otherwise used 'Clarissa' correctly.

Early discovery loop cost time and clarity: 'it means we're moving 21 bedroom apartments, is that correct?' and then a full back-and-forth to establish whether the two-bedroom was the origin or the destination ('Oh, no, no, no, the one that you're current that your address, your apartment 3275').

Customer had to re-ask two numbers she had already given — 'I'm sorry you said it was $75 charge for the travel fee, correct?' and 'it was $102 an hour per mover and then for three people would it be $306' — a sign the pricing block was delivered faster than it was absorbed.
top_strength: The discovery was the best part of this call and it was genuinely thorough — closer to a walkthrough than a phone intake. Joanna captured all three addresses including one the customer had not submitted ('the number is 2770 Summer Street'), floors and elevator access at every stop, furniture inventory room by room including the office ('do you have any extra furniture here at your apartment? Like for office, then standing desk chairs, filing cabinets, or about balcony furniture'), box counts at both origins, oversized and fragile screens, and then walk distance measured properly with the school-bus equivalent at all three locations: 'one school bus is about thirty to forty feet. How many school buses do you think that would be in terms of distance?' She then asked the stressor question verbatim to standard — 'do you have any special instructions concerns or stressors about moving in general that you want me to take note of at this time?' — which is what surfaced the monitors and the wall-mounted TV, and she resolved that one on the spot and in Einstein's favor: 'We can help you unmount it. That's totally fine. That's already part of the service so you don't have to pay extra for that.' The pricing and clock blocks were near-complete: Saturday rate at $102 per mover per hour, $306 for three, the $70 one-time travel fee called out as the only thing outside the hourly, inclusions, disassembly/reassembly, all four differentiators (No Worries at $2,000, Meet Your Mover with 'we don't take daily contract to workers,' On-Time Guarantee, and the no-hidden-fees list), then clock-starts-on-site, 2.5 hour minimum, 15-minute increments, and 'Does that make sense?' — which earned an explicit 'That makes sense. Yup.' She also volunteered real money-saving advice unprompted and did the math correctly: 'if it's on a Sunday, it's $96 per hour per mover. So, for three guys is $288. So pretty much we're saving about $18 per hour,' which checks out against her own '$100 to $140' claim across a six-to-eight hour move. Her quote arithmetic was also clean — $306 x 6 + $70 = $1,906 and $306 x 8 + $70 = $2,518, both stated accurately.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: she had a genuinely warm, well-informed buyer on a date she had just described as the fastest-booking day of the week, said 'we don't take deposits' — and then let the call end on 'I'll talk to my [roommate].' That is a booked job she talked herself out of by never asking. The line she needed, right after the no-deposit mention, was: 'Clarissa, since there's no deposit and no cost to hold it, let me put you on the schedule for Saturday the 26th right now — if your roommate wants to change anything, one phone call and it's moved, but at least the truck is yours instead of somebody else's.' Ask for the date, then handle the roommate as a change order, not a gate. Second priority, and this one matters for the estimate-accuracy work: the range moved the wrong direction. She said two one-bedrooms run five to seven hours with two movers, then quoted six to eight with three. If the third mover is worth adding, the range should tighten and shift down; if the walk-distance unknowns justify padding, say so out loud as a separate line item — 'three movers puts the work itself at four and a half to six hours, and I'm adding a buffer on top because we haven't measured the walk at the new place, so I'll quote you six to eight and my expectation is we come in under it.' Right now the padding is invisible, which is exactly the conservative-hedging pattern that keeps actuals outside the 20 percent band. Third: the Save Your Ass speech was started and abandoned. She got as far as 'how prepared we are on' and went to parking instead. On a two-origin move with roughly forty boxes and a customer who already volunteered that she wants to help, this was the highest-value ninety seconds available — 'Before Saturday, get everything off the walls, empty the loose stuff out of drawers, and stack the boxes by the door of each apartment. Anything that fits in your car, take it over yourself. On a six-hour job, that kind of prep routinely saves an hour, which is three hundred dollars off your final bill. Does that make sense?' Smaller fixes: give hours and a direct number before hanging up, tell her to reply to the email with corrections, ask 'any other questions before I let you go?', and check the name on the way out — closing with 'Thanks Teresa' after fifteen good minutes with Clarissa is an avoidable dent.
phone_presence_notes: Consistently patient and reassuring — 'No, it's okay. Take your time,' 'that's okay, no worries,' 'I understand sometimes it's just really the day that you can take a day off' — and the customer closed warmly with 'I appreciate all the helps' and 'thank you so much, Joanna,' though there was no humor or real rapport moment and the wrong-name goodbye undercut an otherwise strong finish.
audio_review_reason: Clarity and pace cannot be judged from this transcript. Multiple stretches come through mangled ('large fraud items,' 'the sri wraps,' 'a Ford guy,' 'are you familiar of the walking business firm,' 'There's no reason securing a spot,' 'Thanks Teresa'), and the customer twice asked her to repeat numbers she had already given — audio is needed to tell whether that is ASR noise or genuine speed-and-diction issues in the pricing block.
